validation_plan.deployment: Owner, on the NAS over SSH, read-only: `docker compose exec monitor printenv FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS` (127.0.0.1 means the default is live) and `docker network inspect <project>_default --format '{{(index .IPAM.Config 0).Gateway}}'` to compare with the configured value (a mismatch means drift). Then open the dashboard Audit page as admin and read the client field of existing login, login_failed and enrolled events: if every entry from different people/devices shows the same 172.x gateway address, the identity collapse is live and CM_FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS must be set per docs/DEPLOY-SYNOLOGY.md:223-229 (and port 8081 bound to 127.0.0.1 on the NAS); distinct real client addresses refute the candidate for this host. No audit traffic is to be sent to the deployment.

title: Base compose (the NAS production file) publishes the unauthenticated, plaintext ntfy server and the plaintext app port on every host interface
description: server/docker-compose.yml is the file the NAS production consumes ('Use existing docker-compose.yml', docs/DEPLOY-SYNOLOGY.md:58). It publishes ntfy as "8090:80" (line 78) and the app as "8080:8080" (line 19) with no host_ip, which Docker renders as 0.0.0.0, and the ntfy service (lines 71-80) carries no auth configuration (no auth-file / auth-default-access, no NTFY_* env, no server.yml mount), so the pinned image's documented default of anonymous read-write access to every topic applies. The NAS guide itself expects contacts to reach this instance directly ('subscribe to their topic URL, e.g. https://nas:8090/cm-relative1', docs/DEPLOY-SYNOLOGY.md:262-263) although nothing in the base compose terminates TLS for ntfy, so that path is plain HTTP. If the operator followed the guide and copied .env.example (CM_NTFY_URL=http://ntfy, .env.example:29; the compose fallback is https://ntfy.sh, docker-compose.yml:34), the app's alert pump posts every ntfy alert to this container (main.py:484-488 -> channels.py:85-88): the message carries the wearer's name, a Google-Maps location link (channels.py:32-35) and, in the Actions header, the raw acknowledge URL (channels.py:83-84). Any device on the NAS's LAN (household, guest Wi-Fi, compromised IoT) or on any network the router forwards 8090 to can therefore (a) subscribe to a contact's topic if it knows or guesses the topic name (validated only as 4-64 chars of [A-Za-z0-9_-], wearers.py:249; ntfy offers no anonymous topic listing, so topic secrecy is the only gate), receive the alert and POST the ack URL to /api/v1/ack/{token} (main.py:339-344 -> do_ack 306-319, possession of the token is the only check) so the contact appears to have acknowledged and tier promotion stops; (b) publish spoofed 'Standby' alerts to a known topic; (c) passively read all alerts and ack URLs on the plaintext 8090 subscription traffic without guessing anything; (d) use the household's push server as an open relay. Calibration: topic-as-capability on an open ntfy is also the posture of the compose default https://ntfy.sh, so the differential introduced by this binding is the plaintext LAN transport, the LAN-wide relay and the loss of the 'private to the host' property the VPS overlay deliberately restores with !override 127.0.0.1 (docker-compose.vps.yml:17-18, 26-27, and its comment at 8-10 that ufw does not protect Docker-published ports). The 8080 publication additionally offers LAN peers a plaintext path to the bearer API, the enrol endpoint and the forwarded-header-trusting listener beside DSM's TLS terminator; the guide acknowledges this and only recommends the 127.0.0.1 bind as an aside (docs/DEPLOY-SYNOLOGY.md:100-102, 227-229). Whether the live NAS still runs the ntfy service, what it binds to, which ntfy CM_NTFY_URL names, and whether any contact uses an ntfy topic are owner-observed facts that decide the real result.
claimed_root_cause: server/docker-compose.yml:77-78 and :18-19 publish the ntfy and app ports without a host_ip (0.0.0.0 on every host interface), and the ntfy service (:71-80) sets no authentication, so the base deployment used on the NAS hands an anonymous read-write push server over plain HTTP, and a plaintext API listener, to every peer on the host's networks; the loopback pinning that the VPS overlay applies (docker-compose.vps.yml:17-18, 26-27) is absent from the file the NAS consumes.

trace.description: `- "8090:80"` with no host_ip publishes the ntfy container's port 80 on all host interfaces (Docker inserts its own DNAT rules, bypassing host firewalls such as ufw, as docker-compose.vps.yml:8-10 notes); a LAN peer reaches ntfy here.

ntfy is started with bare `serve` and no auth-file, auth-default-access, NTFY_* environment or server.yml mount anywhere in the service (lines 71-80), so the image's documented default of anonymous read-write access to every topic applies.

The example env the NAS guide copies (`cp .env.example .env`, docs/DEPLOY-SYNOLOGY.md:47) points the app's ntfy delivery at this bundled container; the compose fallback when the variable is absent is https://ntfy.sh (docker-compose.yml:34).

For every due contact the pump builds ack_url = f"{PUBLIC_URL}/api/v1/ack/{raw_token}" and renders the alert (wearer name, detector, location link) before calling the contact's channel (lines 484-488).

The alert is POSTed to f"{base_url}/{quote(topic)}" (line 86) with `Actions: http, Acknowledge, <ack_url>, method=POST, clear=true`; every subscriber of that topic on the open ntfy, and any passive observer of the plaintext 8090 subscription stream, receives the raw ack URL and the alert content.

The only check is possession of the token (lookup_ack_token(hash) + unresolved): a LAN subscriber who obtained the URL records the ack for the contact (record_ack, line 314), which the escalation treats as that contact responding and tier promotion stops; conversely a LAN publisher can push spoofed 'Standby' alerts into the same topic.

evidence.description: `- "8080:8080"` with no host IP: the plaintext API/dashboard listener is published on all interfaces of the NAS (the owner's local copy uses host port 8081 per docs/DEPLOY-SYNOLOGY.md:85).
`- "8090:80"` with no host IP: the ntfy listener is published on all interfaces.
`command: serve` — the whole ntfy service (lines 71-80) has no auth-related configuration or environment.
`CM_NTFY_URL: ${CM_NTFY_URL:-https://ntfy.sh}` — the compose fallback differs from .env.example, so which ntfy carries alerts depends on the NAS .env.

The overlay's comment (lines 8-10) states Docker publishes ports through its own iptables chains so `ufw deny 8080` does not protect a published port; the overlay pins monitor and ntfy to 127.0.0.1 with !override (lines 17-18, 26-27), a control the base file lacks.
NAS guide: Container Manager project with source 'Use existing docker-compose.yml' — the base file is the production manifest.
'`ntfy` on port 8090 (self-hosted push; optional — remove from docker-compose.yml if you use ntfy.sh or Telegram only)' — removal is optional and manual.

'The `ntfy` container needs no account: contacts install the ntfy app and subscribe to their topic URL, e.g. `https://nas:8090/cm-relative1`' — the guide expects contacts to reach 8090 directly, while nothing in the base compose terminates TLS for ntfy.

'Port 8080 is published on the NAS, so LAN clients could spoof the forwarding header — bind it to the NAS (`127.0.0.1:8080:8080`) if that matters on your network' — the LAN exposure of the app port is acknowledged and the loopback bind is left optional.
`_NTFY_RE = ^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{4,64}$` — contact topics may be as short as 4 characters, so topic secrecy, the only gate on an open ntfy, can be weak.
Alert body includes `Location: https://maps.google.com/?q=<lat,lon>` and the wearer's name — the data a LAN subscriber or plaintext observer receives.

blockers: The live NAS compose project cannot be observed here: whether the ntfy service is still present, what the published ports actually bind to (0.0.0.0 vs 127.0.0.1 vs a LAN address) and whether the router or a DSM reverse-proxy rule exposes 8090 beyond the LAN are owner-observed facts; docs/DEPLOY-SYNOLOGY.md:262 suggests contacts are meant to reach 8090 directly.

The effective CM_NTFY_URL on the NAS (.env is out of bounds for this audit; the compose fallback is https://ntfy.sh while .env.example says http://ntfy) decides whether the open ntfy carries real alerts and raw ack URLs or is only an open relay.
Whether any enrolled contact actually has an ntfy topic (vs Telegram/email only) is database state visible only to the owner; without ntfy contacts the pump never posts to the instance.

ntfy's anonymous read-write default is taken from the vendor's documentation for the auth-default-access setting, not re-verified against image v2.28.0 under this run's no-network policy; the owner's rendered config observation closes this.
Trust level of the NAS's LAN (flat home network with guests/IoT vs an isolated VLAN) is an environmental fact that scales the likelihood.

validation_plan.local: From a checkout, render the manifest without starting anything: `cd server && docker compose -f docker-compose.yml config` — confirm that `services.monitor.ports` and `services.ntfy.ports` render with `published: "8080"`/`"8090"` and no `host_ip` key (meaning 0.0.0.0), and that `services.ntfy` has no `environment` entries and no server.yml volume. For comparison `docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.vps.yml config` must show `host_ip: 127.0.0.1` on both. The pytest fixtures in server/tests/conftest.py use a FakeChannel and do not model ntfy, so no in-process test applies.
validation_plan.deployment: On the NAS over SSH (observation only, no traffic): (1) `docker ps --format '{{.Names}} {{.Ports}}'` — a line such as `cryomonitor-ntfy-1 0.0.0.0:8090->80/tcp` (or `sudo ss -ltnp | grep -E ':(8081|8080|8090)\b'` showing `0.0.0.0:`/`*:`) confirms all-interface publishing; `127.0.0.1:` refutes it. (2) `cd /volume1/docker/cryomonitor && docker compose config | sed -n '/ntfy:/,$p'` — confirm the ntfy service is present and has no NTFY_AUTH_FILE / NTFY_AUTH_DEFAULT_ACCESS environment and no server.yml mount. (3) `docker compose exec monitor printenv CM_NTFY_URL` — `http://ntfy` means the bundled instance receives alerts and ack URLs; `https://ntfy.sh` means it is only an open relay. (4) In the dashboard, check whether any contact has an ntfy topic and how long those topics are. (5) In the router and DSM Login Portal → Reverse Proxy, confirm nothing forwards or proxies to 8090. Remediation if confirmed: pin both to loopback or the NAS's LAN/VPN address in the compose file (`127.0.0.1:8090:80`, `127.0.0.1:8080:8080`), publish ntfy to contacts only through DSM's TLS reverse proxy, and configure ntfy auth (`NTFY_AUTH_FILE`, `NTFY_AUTH_DEFAULT_ACCESS=deny-all`, per-topic write-only for the app and read-only for contacts) or drop the service when Telegram/email suffice; fix docs/DEPLOY-SYNOLOGY.md:262 accordingly.
